resources.title: Fieldwork enquiry assessment
paragraphs_in_document_order: Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A

Assess an individual structured fieldwork enquiry from the LAUNCH pair in forty minutes. Each pupil uses their checked anonymous Weeks 4–5 records or the complete supplied practice data. This lesson can assess enquiry write-up skills even when real data is incomplete. It cannot establish missing real fieldwork collection.

Weekly objective, LAUNCH Weekly - Autumn!C59: Fieldwork enquiry write-up (Dec). Theme: Identity & Belonging. Unit: Geography: place, settlement & urbanisation. Assessment, LAUNCH - Autumn!J11: F: map/GIS skills checks.  S: fieldwork enquiry write-up (Dec).

Visible finish: one enquiry with question, method, data table, graph, two numerical findings that answer the question, and evaluation of one limit plus a linked improvement. Evidence ID HUM-LAUNCH-A2-W07-E1. Actual outcomes remain blank.

Prepare the chosen route, evidence form, S1–S3 and word mat. Offer White or Pink paper. Check each learner’s prior data, question, method, category key, units and graph before arrival. Use a named-source-free copy with the site described by type only. Keep the source private and do not bring names, map pins or identifying photographs into this pack.

If prior data is missing or cannot be checked, use S1–S3 for the full write-up. Label it supplied fictional practice data. Do not fill gaps in actual data with invented values. If both sources are used, label each table, graph and claim separately. A comparison is optional only when methods and units are compatible.

Two pupils, L01 and L02. Quiet reading, pointing, writing, typing, exact scribing or the usual aid are valid. No cold calling or required reading aloud. Choose routes by current need. All routes cover the same six sections. Record what the pupil did and what an adult or prepared resource supplied.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Introduce the assessed write-up and identify the source of the data.
Private arrival check. Quiet reading, processing time and usual aids.
Retrieve sample, category, table, axes and cautious claims from earlier work.
Share all six sections and individual success criteria.
Model a separate four-plot pilot, then cover it. Do not model S2 findings.
Check the six-part structure. Hinge B: a route sample cannot describe a whole town.
Twelve minutes: question, source, method, table and graph. Check progress halfway. Record supplied material and actual support.
Ten minutes: two numerical findings, conclusion, limitation and linked improvement. Each pupil uses their own words.
Three minutes: review six sections. Adult reply and one NS, then keep the learner’s correction.
Two minutes: collect individual work and source/graph status. Record unresolved gaps.
Word mat available throughout. Private explanations and usual aids.
Hidden adult brief. Prompt ladder and honest support/evidence recording.

Keep the pilot demonstration separate from S2. Cover it before the individual write-up. Staff answers stay out of view. Allow clarification of directions and usual access support, then record each prompt. A partner’s answer is not evidence for both learners. Keep the first response and any revision.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A

Use the six-criterion rubric on Staff Answers: question, method, table, graph, findings and evaluation, each 0–2. Total out of 12 is a local task profile, not an award grade. Record criterion evidence and actual support. A supplied graph can show graph reading and checking; it does not show independent construction. A supplied data set can show interpretation and evaluation; it does not show actual collection.

“There are ten sampled plots in each section. Does the pattern describe the whole town?” No. It describes these route sections only. Ask the pupil to point to “sample” and choose a smaller claim. Any answer supplied by an adult is recorded as support. Reteach after the first attempt when possible.

A survey or planning assistant reports how data was obtained and the limits of a claim. Offer the pupil’s authentic enquiry explanation to the Communication portfolio. Record an adult audience reply, one NS and own-colour or usual supported response before R. E records actual banking only. VF, WS, I, NS, // and ? may be used privately; reading aloud is never required.

resources.title: Fieldwork source cards
paragraphs_in_document_order: Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
White paper version | Read quietly. Point, write, type or use a scribe. No reading aloud is required.
SUPPLIED PRACTICE DATA. This is a fictional route through an inland residential neighbourhood. No real place or real collection is represented.
Enquiry question: How does land use differ between two sections of a residential route?

The model survey records the first ten plots on one side of section A and the first ten on one side of section B along a single planned route. A plot is one separately bounded site. The two sections do not overlap.

The model uses one primary land-use code per plot: H homes; S services; W workshops; O open space. Mixed use would be coded by its main visible use and marked for a later check. No mixed-use uncertainty is entered in this practice set.

The stated model observation is one dry weekday morning, in one visit. A recorder enters each plot code in a table, totals each category and checks that each section has ten entries. A graph then compares the counts.
Say “The supplied data describes…” when using this set. Do not say that you collected it. Use the method above to evaluate what this model could show.
Name the question, site type, unit, sample size and coding rule. Mark the source as supplied. If using your own data, describe what actually happened instead.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
White paper version | Read quietly. Point, write, type or use a scribe. No reading aloud is required.
SUPPLIED PRACTICE DATA. Each row is one model plot in each section. The codes use the S1 key. These are not real addresses.
Check: each plot appears once. Count plots, not people or floor area. Keep both sections separate. Ten is the total for each section; twenty is the total across the route.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
White paper version | Read quietly. Point, write, type or use a scribe. No reading aloud is required.
SUPPLIED PRACTICE DATA. Use a grouped bar graph for S2. Plot two bars for each use. Start at zero, use one-plot steps and label a zero value.
Suggested title: Sampled land use in two route sections. Vertical axis: Number of sampled plots. Horizontal axis: Main land use. Key: A solid; B hatched. The evidence form provides a blank grid.
Do the bar heights match S2? Are the section labels clear? Does the title say sampled? Does the graph use an even scale? If an adult supplies a graph, mark that support and check two bars yourself.

These first ten plots may miss other kinds of street. One side of each section may differ from the other side. A visible main-use code may miss uses inside a building. One visit cannot show changes over time.

Choose one limit. Explain how it could affect a finding. Suggest a change that addresses it, such as more route sections with a planned selection rule or checking uncertain codes with a second recorder.

SUPPLIED PRACTICE DATA. This is a fictional route through an inland residential neighbourhood. No real place or real collection is represented.
Enquiry question: How does land use differ between two sections of a residential route?

The model survey records the first ten plots on one side of section A and the first ten on one side of section B along a single planned route. A plot is one separately bounded site. The two sections do not overlap.

The model uses one primary land-use code per plot: H homes; S services; W workshops; O open space. Mixed use would be coded by its main visible use and marked for a later check. No mixed-use uncertainty is entered in this practice set.

The stated model observation is one dry weekday morning, in one visit. A recorder enters each plot code in a table, totals each category and checks that each section has ten entries. A graph then compares the counts.
Say “The supplied data describes…” when using this set. Do not say that you collected it. Use the method above to evaluate what this model could show.

resources.title: Fieldwork assessment guidance
paragraphs_in_document_order: Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A

Keep this sheet away from the pupil assessment view. Use a separate four-plot pilot to model structure, then collect each pupil’s own response. Do not read out the S2 model findings before assessment.
Answerable question linked to the data
Source, unit, sample and selection/coding described
Accurate values, headings, unit and totals
Accurate graph or supported checking with labels, scale and key
One valid pattern or weak evidence
Two numerical findings and a bounded answer
Limit, effect and a linked improvement explained

Score 0 where no valid evidence is yet shown. Record a score for each part, exact evidence and actual support. Total /12 is a local task profile, not a qualification grade. Use the same criteria across routes; record independence separately.

For a supplied table or graph, ask the pupil to check entries, label it and use it in their answer. A high reasoning score with support does not establish independent construction. No supplied set proves actual data collection.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Homes A7/B3; services A1/B4; workshops A0/B1; open space A2/B2. Each section totals 10, route total 20. Hinge answer B: the sample covers two route sections only.

Homes differ by 4 plots, services by 3, workshops by 1; open space is equal. Homes are 70% of A and 30% of B, a 40-percentage-point gap. These are proportions of sampled plots, not population or land area.

Access option: give a crop or print of the graph only, after recording it as supplied. Keep the model findings and rubric page away from the pupil view. Assess their checks and reading, and leave independent graph construction unclaimed.
Tuesday 15 December 2026 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Question: How does land use differ between two sections of a residential route?

Method: I used the supplied fictional S1–S2 data. The model records the first ten plots on one side of each section, one main-use code per plot, during one dry weekday morning. The unit is a plot. I did not collect this data.

Findings: A has 7 home plots and B has 3, so A has 4 more. B has 4 service plots and A has 1, so B has 3 more. Both have 2 open-space plots. In these sampled sections, A has a greater share of homes and B a greater share of services.

Evaluation: The first ten plots on one side may miss other kinds of street. The pattern may change elsewhere. I would sample further sections using a planned selection rule and the same categories. That would improve coverage, though it would still be a sample. These counts cannot show why the pattern occurs.

Accept other accurate count comparisons, a cautious conclusion and a justified limitation with a matching improvement. If pupils use their own data, mark against that source and method. Do not require the S2 numbers or a fictional method.

Give one actual adult reply and NS. Keep the learner’s own change or usual supported response. Record R only after that exchange and E only after banking. Leave unfinished evidence visible. Award requirements remain a separate masked staff check.
